item.title: Stolen childhoods: Why Bangladesh must scrap section 19 of the Child Marriage Act. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Imagine the combined population of the ASEAN nations, or that of Latin America and the Caribbean. Nearly as many women and girls alive in 2026 were married as children worldwide -- an estimated 650 million, including 44 million in Bangladesh.
Today, the world observes the inaugural International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage, following a United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) resolution adopted in September proclaiming November 27 as the day to galvanize global efforts against this crisis. While the observance offers a vital opportunity for collective action, Bangladesh faces a sobering reality: It has one of the highest rates of child marriage in the world.
According to the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, the proportion of women aged 20--24 who were married before the age of 18 declined from 51.4% in 2019 to 47.2%, marking slow and modest progress. However, the survey reveals an alarming reversal among younger adolescents: 38.9% of girls aged 15--19 are currently married, up from 32.9% in 2019. This six-percentage-point increase erases 13 years of hard-won progress, taking the country back to the 39% rate recorded in 2006. Globally, around 12 million girls are married before turning 18 every year.
South Asia bears the heaviest burden, with roughly 285 million women and girls who were married as children -- about 45% of the global total. While India has the highest absolute number because of its population size, Bangladesh ranks among the countries with the highest prevalence of child marriage.
As we mark this UN-designated day, we must confront the harsh realities robbing Bangladeshi girls of their childhoods. Too many adolescents remain trapped in a vicious cycle in which early marriage leads to premature pregnancies, jeopardizing maternal and neonatal health, and contributing to child malnutrition -- threatening the very future of our nation.
A major driver of this crisis is a regressive legal loophole introduced in 2017. While countries generally replace archaic laws with more progressive and modern legislation, Bangladesh took a step backwards when it passed the Child Marriage Restraint Act (CMRA) 2017, replacing the colonial-era 1929 law but undermining the universal minimum marriage age of 18. Section 19 of the 2017 Act allows child marriage below the age of 18 under undefined "special circumstances" and with court approval.
From the outset, rights advocates and the media warned that the provision could undermine the law. At the time, the government dismissed these concerns, assuring stakeholders that the enforcement rules to be introduced later would impose strict restrictions on the provision. However, when the CMRA Rules were issued in 2018, they failed to introduce meaningful safeguards.
The MICS 2025 findings now lay bare the cost of this failure. In a country proud of its economic and infrastructural progress, nearly two in five girls aged 15-19 are married. This regression comes even as global child marriage prevalence has declined by 15% over the past decade, from one in four girls (25%) to roughly one in five (21%), representing 25 million fewer child marriages.
Along with India, Pakistan, and parts of sub-Saharan Africa, Bangladesh continues to bear a disproportionate share of the global burden. Meanwhile, in Latin America and the Caribbean, where informal unions are common, progress has stagnated for 25 years, putting the region on track to surpass South Asia in child marriage prevalence by 2030.
Child marriage has devastating consequences. It cuts short girls' education, limits their economic independence, threatens their physical and mental health, and exposes them to domestic and sexual violence, depriving them of their fundamental freedoms.
To be fair, the CMRA 2017 and its 2018 Rules have provided a foundational framework for interventions, including during the Covid-19 pandemic. Public awareness and law enforcement efforts have improved, while communities increasingly use national helplines, including 109, 1098, and 999 to report and prevent impending child marriages.
However, these positive efforts have been undermined by several fundamental flaws in the legislation:
Rather than closing the loophole, the 2018 Rules have widened it, leaving minors vulnerable to forced and premature marriages.
It is better late than never. Bangladesh must urgently review and amend Section 19 of the CMRA 2017 and overhaul the ambiguous 2018 Rules. A country approaching graduation from the least developed country (LDC) category cannot afford to lose its future workforce and leadership to a cycle of early marriage, unplanned pregnancies, and childhood malnutrition.
The UNGA resolution adopted last September calls on member states to implement comprehensive, multisectoral national strategies, invest in quality education -- including opportunities for married girls to return to school -- and empower women and girls.
If Bangladesh is serious about honouring the spirit of this inaugural International Day, it must begin by fixing its laws and guaranteeing adolescent girls the childhood, health, and future they deserve.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Powering ahead sustainably. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It is safe to say that despite ambitions for renewable energy projects, for years, overlapping jurisdictions, sluggish grid approvals, and regulatory ambiguity have held such projects back.
To that end, with the gazetting of the Special Solar Power Installation Act, 2026 earlier this week, the renewable energy sector, especially solar, should at least have the law on its side to power ahead. By granting the new law overriding authority against conflicting regulations, the state has removed the most glaring legal excuses for inaction.
Scaling up solar energy offers an immediate, structural lifeline. Because Bangladesh’s peak electricity consumption occurs during hot, sunny afternoons, driven by industrial operations, irrigation, and cooling, solar generation aligns naturally with daytime demand spikes.
While it is unrealistic to expect Bangladesh to switch to renewable energy sources overnight, replacing expensive imported furnace oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) with domestic solar power will eventually lower generation costs, ease pressure on our foreign currency reserves, and insulate the economy from global energy shocks.
Expanding solar generation beyond conventional rooftops to floating arrays on water bodies and agro-voltaic systems on farmland is also precisely the kind of pragmatic innovation a land-scarce nation such as ours requires.
Yet, in Bangladesh, a progressive statute is only the opening chapter and the real battle is fought against bureaucratic inertia and rent-seeking on the ground. Without strict, transparent oversight, laws have historically invited politically connected cronyism, and this is what must be avoided.
Bangladesh cannot afford yet another well-intentioned law that stalls. The onus is now to enforce transparent procurement, finalize rules without delay, and ensure every watt promised on paper actually reaches our homes and industries.

item.title: We are losing the fight against child marriage. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
That 38.9% of adolescent girls aged 15 to 19 in Bangladesh are now married -- a six-percentage-point surge since 2019 that drags our nation back to 2006 levels -- is nothing if not a tragedy.
Even more alarming is that marriages among girls under 15 have risen to 9.7%, with 51 of the country’s 64 districts recording increases.
The data, as presented by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) should shock us to our cores. Every child forced into premature marriage represents a stolen childhood, an unfinished education, and heightened exposure to maternal mortality, domestic violence, and intergenerational poverty.
Child marriage is never a harmless cultural compromise or a benign survival strategy but a systemic violation of fundamental human rights that inflicts lifelong trauma.
For Bangladesh as a whole, this crisis represents immense damage to its human potential, sidelining half of our youth from the workforce and undermining decades of progress in public health, gender equality, and economic development.
While economic distress, inflation, and climate displacement continue to push vulnerable families toward desperate choices, institutional complacency and legal loopholes have also allowed this practice to flourish unchecked.
Ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early, and Forced Marriage on November 27, routine awareness campaigns and hollow promises will no longer suffice.
The government must treat this crisis with uncompromising urgency. This starts by closing legal loopholes, enforcing strict registration and prosecution, and expanding social safety nets to keep girls in classrooms.
Bangladesh speaks of progressing as a nation, but no nation can claim to be moving forward while allowing its daughters to be sacrificed to the past.

item.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the US-China AI competition, and the US economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?
The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: Central processing units, or CPUs.
GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.
As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier:
GPUs vs CPUs
The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.
A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.
From pretty pictures to AI data centres
Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.
In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.
The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs.
AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.
Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.
Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.
AI takes off
In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.
The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including US-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google, and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centres composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.
These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable, and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code, and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.
Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.
AI ‘arms race’
Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the US government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centres require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.
The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.
Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry.
Jeffrey Young is Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

item.title: The institutional failure behind graduate unemployment. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is a weird waiting room in Bangladesh where nobody has an appointment, nobody knows when a name will be called, and nobody is sure the door will open.
Its occupants are young, educated. They have studied and competed, only to discover that the labour market has a condition they cannot satisfy: Experience. They need a job to gain experience, but need experience to get a job. The waiting room grows as the economy claims to progress.
This is not merely the disappointment of graduates. It is the story of a country better at producing qualifications than organizing opportunities.
A recent study by the Power and Participation Research Center (PPRC) puts youth unemployment among people aged 15 to 29 at 8.07%. The rate rises to 13.5% for bachelor's degree holders and 20.4% for female graduates. Of the country's 2.62 million unemployed people, 885,000 are university graduates.
Even those who find work often enter an insecure world: 92.7% of working young people are employed in the informal sector. A degree no longer reliably signals a route into economic independence.
The familiar explanation is that graduates lack the skills employers need. Curricula can be disconnected from industry, practical learning uneven, and communication and technological abilities underdeveloped. But the skills argument has become a convenient hiding place for systemic failure.
It asks why young people are not ready for work without asking why workplaces will not help them become ready. Employers advertise entry-level jobs requiring experience; universities celebrate graduation without meaningful professional exposure; training centres issue certificates whose value employers rarely test. Everyone produces an output, but nobody owns the transition.
A functioning labour market needs more than graduates on one side and vacancies on the other. It needs a bridge: Employers willing to train, institutions aware of local demand, banks prepared to finance viable ideas, and public agencies that make enterprise possible.
This is the missing middle in Bangladesh's employment story. Policies announce targets and individuals show initiative, but the organizations connecting ambition with opportunity remain fragmented or inaccessible. People are told to become employable, while the institutions responsible for employment are rarely held accountable.
Consider the first-job paradox. A graduate cannot arrive with the experience of someone who has spent years in an industry. Experience must be built, and that requires employers to accept some risk and invest in training.
Paid internships, apprenticeships, supervised placements, and industry-linked university projects should be essential parts of education, with real responsibilities. Employers must also distinguish specialist vacancies from genuine entry-level roles.
A first job should be a starting point, not a test applicants are structurally unable to pass. Universities should assess applied knowledge, not just examination performance.
The waiting room is even more crowded for women. A female graduate may have the same qualifications as a male colleague but face a narrower geography of opportunity.
Unsafe transport, inadequate childcare, harassment, discriminatory recruitment, and unpaid care expectations can turn an apparently open vacancy into an inaccessible one. The 20.4% unemployment rate among female graduates cannot be reduced to individual skills or confidence.
Entrepreneurship schemes are equally inadequate if women seeking loans are asked for property documents they do not own or a husband's signature. Banks must assess business viability rather than reproduce inequality through lending procedures.
For young people who want to create jobs rather than wait for them, the route is hardly easier. Starting a small enterprise can mean navigating registration, licences, taxation, bank requirements, and repeated visits to public offices. When 80% of young people report delays and bribery in accessing government services, administrative friction becomes a tax on initiative, paid in time and money.
A young entrepreneur may have a sound idea but no land for collateral, no credit history or influential connection. The state praises innovation while its procedures make the first step prohibitively expensive. Simplified registration, transparent timelines, accessible credit, and accountable one-stop services would matter more than another startup slogan.
The contradiction is visible beyond major cities. Regions possess assets that could support local jobs if the missing links were built. Rajshahi produces mangoes, but inadequate storage and processing allow value to disappear after harvest. Noakhali grows soybeans, while limited processing restricts the benefits retained locally. Underused space at hi-tech parks raises a basic question: Why build infrastructure without ensuring that businesses, workers, and investment are ready to occupy it?
This calls for a different way of measuring development. A district should not be judged only by roads, buildings, training centres or industrial facilities announced. It should also be judged by local value addition, sustainable jobs, post-training employment, and women's participation.
Local governments, universities, employers, banks and training providers should map their area's economic possibilities. Their performance should be measured through job placement, retention, wage progression, business survival and access to finance, not seminars held or certificates issued. Public incentives should reward firms that train and retain first-time workers, rather than those that merely promise to do so.
The informal economy deserves equal attention. It provides livelihoods for millions and cannot be formalized overnight. But the fact that 92.7% of working youth are employed informally should make policy-makers reconsider what they celebrate as job creation.
Someone without predictable income, written terms, paid leave, insurance or protection against arbitrary dismissal may be employed statistically and insecure in practice. Freelancers and platform workers need fair payment, banking access, and social protection. Formalization should not bury small businesses in paperwork. It should make decent work easier to achieve and sustain.
Nor should Bangladesh assume that economic growth will eventually solve the problem. Growth can coexist with graduate unemployment when investment concentrates in sectors generating few jobs. The demographic advantage is not a permanent asset waiting to be collected. It is a window that can narrow.
A young population becomes an economic dividend only when education, investment, technology, enterprise, and labour institutions work together. Otherwise, a generation of potential contributors risks becoming a generation of postponed lives.
The consequences extend beyond household income. Long unemployment delays independence and family responsibilities, drains confidence and weakens the belief that merit offers a route forward. Families that sacrificed to educate their children may discover that a degree brings neither mobility nor security. Repeatedly closed doors can turn frustration into distrust of institutions and public promises. The loss is not confined to an unemployed individual. It includes resources invested in education, productive capacity left unused and the credibility of a development model that measures progress without asking who gets to participate.
Bangladesh does not need to tell its young people to wait patiently, collect another certificate or become entrepreneurs alone. It needs to make the waiting room smaller.
Employers must open genuine entry routes, universities connect learning with practice, banks recognise viable enterprise beyond traditional collateral, and public agencies treat transparency and time as obligations. That should be the measure of progress, not promises.
Young people are not asking the country to guarantee every ambition. They are asking for a fair chance to begin. A nation that teaches its children to prepare for the future must build a future in which their preparation has somewhere to go.
HM Nazmul Alam is an academic, journalist, and political analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he is teaching at IUBAT.

item.title: India separates Hasina’s return from extradition. [ dawn ]
item.description:
NEW DELHI: India’s foreign ministry said on Wednesday that former Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s plan to return voluntarily to her home country is separate from Dhaka’s extradition request.

Hasina has said that she plans to return home from more than two years of exile in India on Dec 16.

The Bangladesh government, however, reiterated that she can only be extradited.

Hasina fled Dhaka after a deadly student uprising against her rule in Aug 2024 and has lived in exile in India since.

This month, she requested a new passport and identity card so she could return from self-imposed exile.

In Bangladesh, she faces a death sentence handed down in her absence last year by a court that convicted her of ordering a crackdown on the student-led uprising.

Indian foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal reiterated that New Delhi is examining the extradition request by Dhaka in line with its established processes.

“The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,” Jaiswal said, responding to a question at a regular media briefing. He did not elaborate.

New tensions have risen in Bangladesh after Dhaka rejected Hasina’s request for a passport that would allow her to return.

item.title: US unveils proposed tariffs on major partners, including EU, China and India. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The United States on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies, including the European Union, China and India, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production — the latest move by US President Donald Trump to remake Washington’s trade relationships.

The duties, proposed at up to 20 per cent, come over allegations that the economies “are promoting production and capacity divorced from the realities of demand and market principles,” a senior US official said on condition of anonymity.

The new tariffs will need to undergo a period of public comment before taking effect, with the official adding that the proposals take existing trade deals into account.

The new levies target some of the United States’ largest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

The US official made specific mention of China, for whom a 20pc tariff is being proposed, the joint-highest for any economy.

In a separate announcement, the US Trade Representative’s office also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.

Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.

The latest move offers some relief for partners that earlier signed tariff deals with the Trump administration, but it could still raise temperatures as the US president prepares to host G20 leaders in Miami in December.

“We don’t expect this to create tension or rancor” at the G20 summit, the senior US official said. “We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements.”

Inflation pressures

Over-capacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.

The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on costs to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.

Affordability was a key issue in recent midterm elections, which saw Trump’s Republican Party swept out of power in both houses of Congress by Democrats.

US consumer inflation came in at 3.7pc year-on-year in September, close to a three-year high as prices are pushed up by the effects of Trump’s war on Iran, tariffs, and the massive AI investment boom.

US Federal Reserve policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-per cent target, say that most price effects of Trump’s previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy — but any new levies could push prices up further.

The new tariffs are likely to come into effect in January at the earliest, the senior US official said.

Trump’s latest duties come after an investigation the US Trade Representative started in March on excess manufacturing capacity and production.

The concern was whether other countries were taking actions deemed “unreasonable or discriminatory,” and if they weighed on US commerce.

The probes came days after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous slew of tariffs, holding that the president did not hold the authority to impose the duties using the law the White House had cited.

Pushback expected

Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among “the most important” actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.”

This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a “hollowing out” of US manufacturing, he added.

The US determination is likely to face strong pushback from China and others, with Beijing long rejecting criticism that it relies too much on exports to boost its economy.

While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.

The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.

In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.

For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail.

item.title: Why Israel should be afraid of the ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar. [ middleeasteye ]
item.description:
Why Israel should be afraid of the ICJ genocide ruling against Myanmar

Submitted by Jonathan Cook on Tue, 11/24/2026 - 10:57
The court's finding against Myanmar undercuts each of Israel's defences over Gaza, and exposes the western states that cheered one verdict while arming the other genocide
Pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrate outside the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague, on 24 May, 2024 (Reuters)
Off

There are many reasons why Israel will be deeply worried by the International Court of Justice's finding on 19 November that the military junta in Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority nearly a decade ago.

The president of the world's highest court, Yuji Iwasawa, concluded that Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and tried to hide its crimes through "extensive destruction of evidence".

During so-called "clearance operations" in 2017, Myanmar's security forces from the Buddhist-majority state of Myanmar killed at least 10,000 Rohingya, a Muslim minority, and drove more than 700,000 from their homes in northern Rakhine state. Most found refuge in Bangladesh.

Entire villages were erased, evidence destroyed by burning bodies and bulldozing sites, and the Rohingya subjected to campaigns of rape and sexual violence. Myanmar failed to prosecute the perpetrators.

So what are the implications for another prominent genocide case being considered by the ICJ, this one brought against Israel by South Africa, and backed by more than a dozen other countries, including Ireland, Belgium, Spain and the Netherlands?

Back in January 2024, just weeks into Israel's onslaught in Gaza, the World Court found a "plausible risk" that Palestinians there were being subjected to genocide.

It also imposed a series of provisional measures on Israel to ensure its military did not commit genocidal acts, that aid was allowed in, that all incitement stopped, and that the destruction of evidence was prevented. Israel ignored all of these obligations.

Intent on show

First, the ICJ ruling against Myanmar has set a legal precedent. It is the first time the court has found a state guilty of genocide. It clears a path for the United Nations court to make the same finding, based on even more damning evidence, against Israel.

The bar for establishing genocide has always been higher than for proving war crimes or crimes against humanity because, critically, it requires demonstrating intent by the state under investigation.

In ruling against Myanmar, the court noted that the regime had encouraged anti-Rohingya hate speech, portraying the minority as "sub-human" and posing a "violent threat". This rhetoric, in the view of the judges, exposed the deeper reasoning behind Myanmar's "clearance operations".

In Israel's case, it should be easier to establish intent than it was with Myanmar. Nine pages of South Africa's 84-page submission (59-67) to the ICJ were quotes from Israeli leaders, from the prime minister down, expressing genocidal intent towards Gaza's civilian population.

As is often pointed out, this was the most publicly confessed crime in history.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu compared Gaza's Palestinians to Amalek. In the Bible, the Israelites are ordered by God to kill every last Amalek man, woman and child, leaving no one alive. In other words, to commit a genocide.

Former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant called the people of Gaza "human animals" and insisted they be denied all food, water and fuel.

President Isaac Herzog declared no one in Gaza, not even its children, to be innocent: "It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It is not true this rhetoric about civilians not aware, not involved. It's absolutely not true."

The record of genocidal incitement by Israel's leadership is indisputable.

Second, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's defence that its violence was a justifiable response - that it was counterterrorism - following violent attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.

The judges ruled that the junta could be pursuing more than one strategy at the same time, and that its military actions to kill rebel fighters could run in parallel to a wider policy of targeting the civilian population.

This is precisely where Israel's narrative is likely to come unstuck.

Israel and its apologists prefer to start the clock with Hamas's one-day breakout on 7 October 2023 from long-besieged Gaza - effectively a concentration camp for Palestinians engineered by Israel over the preceding decades.

Hamas's short, bloody attack inside Israel did not initiate the violence. As the ICJ found in a separate advisory opinion in 2024, Israel has committed crimes systematically against the Palestinian people for decades - and long before October 2023.

That includes an illegal and brutal military occupation, the forced transfer of Palestinians from their homes so Jewish settlers can colonise their land, the prolonged siege of Gaza, and a violent regime of apartheid rule against Palestinians.

More specifically, Israel has claimed its carpet-bombing of Gaza, and its destruction of essential civilian infrastructure - homes, hospitals, schools, government offices, bakeries, agricultural land - is warranted by its efforts to "eradicate Hamas".

In the Myanmar ruling, the ICJ showed it is likely to give short shrift to such rationalisations.

Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide. In fact, it could do so precisely to remove the possibility of resistance to its war crimes and make the task of committing genocide easier.

Cover story

Third, Myanmar argued that, if its goal was genocide, it could have killed far more Rohingya than it actually did. Estimates are that the junta's actions most likely killed between 1 and 2 percent of the Rohingya people.

The ICJ found, in accordance with the 1948 Genocide Convention, that genocide is not a numbers game. Once intent to destroy a people in whole or part is established, other practices - such as preventing births, forcibly displacing the population, and making their lands uninhabitable - also qualify as genocide.

Israel and its apologists have wilfully sought to mislead about the convention's definition, treating the Holocaust as the only model of what a genocide looks like.

Israel's genocide in Gaza continues. So must the protests
Read More »

Their argument rests heavily on the false idea that genocide is indeed about numbers, and that Israel would have wiped out everyone in Gaza were it actually bent on genocide.

Netanyahu has regularly articulated this sentiment. In August 2025, for example, he told a press conference: "If we had wanted to commit genocide, it would have taken exactly one afternoon."

Again, the ICJ is unlikely to entertain this as a defence.

Netanyahu's logic intentionally obscures the obvious fact that, in an age of international law, states like Myanmar and Israel have a vested interest in concealing their genocidal intent both by carrying out their crimes incrementally and by offering military rationales as a cover story.

Based on the Rohingya ruling, the number of dead in Gaza is sufficient to qualify as genocidal violence. The known death toll, at nearly 75,000, is more than 3 percent of Gaza's population - and double the percentage of known Rohingya fatalities at the hands of Myanmar's junta.

The Gaza estimates, however, are likely to be a severe undercount, given that many Palestinians were buried under rubble or vaporised by US-supplied 2,000lb bombs. It is also a count of those killed by Israeli weaponry, not those who have died as a result of the dire conditions Israel has engineered in the enclave.

The Israeli military's own assessments are also damning. According to their tally, revealed in August 2025, more than four in five of the dead were civilians, not Palestinian fighters.

Genetic harm

Fourth, the ICJ found that Myanmar had committed genocide in three of the convention's five categories: the mass killing; causing serious bodily and mental harm through torture, physical injuries and sexual violence; and preventing births within the group by targeting children and reproductive organs.

Israel has clearly committed crimes on a significant scale in these same three categories, plus it has violated an additional, fourth category of the convention.

As noted earlier, both numerically and proportionally, Israel has killed more Palestinians than Myanmar killed Rohingya. UN bodies have repeatedly found that Israel has caused serious bodily and mental harm to the people of Gaza.

Nearly one in ten Palestinians there are known to have been maimed by Israel's attacks, and nearly everyone has been left with deep mental scars from Israel's relentless bombing campaigns, the equivalent of unleashing at least six Hiroshimas over the tiny enclave.

In addition, thousands of Palestinians - men, women and children - have been seized from Gaza and held in detention camps where torture and sexual violence are reported to be rife. Inmates often emerge severely malnourished.

In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel was deliberately targeting children in Gaza. It said these acts "form part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza by targeting their children".

Independent witnesses, such as international doctors volunteering in Gaza, have testified that soldiers appear to be playing horrifying games in which they compete with each other to show off their prowess as snipers.

Each day, according to the doctors, the soldiers target a different body part: the neck, the abdomen, the testicles.

The ICJ also has plenty of evidence to find against Israel in an additional category in the Genocide Convention, that of creating conditions destructive to life.

In Myanmar's case, the ICJ ruled that evidence the Rohingya had been confined in internment camps where they were denied basic healthcare was not sufficient to meet this fourth category.

In Israel's case, by contrast, Palestinians have not only been denied access to health services. Israel has systematically gone about destroying the entire healthcare system and blocking the entry of medicines and medical equipment.

It has subjected the people of Gaza to sustained starvation, creating widespread malnutrition that scientists warn will cause lasting genetic harm.

It has blocked the entry of equipment to repair water and sewage systems Israel has destroyed, exposing the people to contaminated groundwater and the spread of disease. It has also blocked tents, blankets and mattresses desperately needed as winter sets in.

As Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory reported on 23 November, by reducing Gaza's buildings to rubble through the use of many tens of thousands of tonnes of explosives, Israel has created a "toxic wasteland", one that will expose the enclave's inhabitants to grave health dangers for "generations to come".

On these and many other grounds, the ICJ can find Israel has violated the Genocide Convention even more comprehensively than Myanmar.

Journalists killed

Fifth, as part of the genocide finding against Myanmar, the World Court factored in a wider context of systematic discrimination by Buddhist majority against the Rohingya that reinforced suspicions of genocidal intent.

These discriminatory policies included eroding the Rohingya's human rights through restrictions on movement and the blocking of humanitarian aid, and limiting married couples to two children.

Other matters served similarly as circumstantial evidence, especially the concealment and destruction of evidence, a failure to prevent civilians from committing atrocities alongside security forces, and a reluctance to prosecute perpetrators.

As noted earlier, the ICJ has already found Israel guilty of operating a decades-old system of apartheid against Palestinians. That included blockading Gaza by land, sea and air for nearly two decades, strictly controlling who could go in or out of the enclave.

Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities

Israel was also forced to admit in 2012 that it had imposed a near-starvation diet on the people of Gaza starting four years earlier. In the words of a close adviser to the prime minister of the time, Ehud Olmert, the goal was "to put the Palestinians on a diet, but not to make them die of hunger".

In 2015, the UN warned that Gaza, under Israel's severe restrictions, would soon become "uninhabitable", that Israel had sought to de-develop the enclave, and that the enclave's aquifers were quickly becoming contaminated by seawater, posing a threat to the health of the population.

Israel has sought to conceal its crimes in Gaza by refusing to allow entry to foreign journalists to report on what is happening there. Meanwhile, it has killed local Palestinian journalists in unprecedented numbers in an attempt to stop them from documenting its crimes.

Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities and has sought to destroy incriminating evidence, including by secretly burying Palestinian victims of its violence in mass graves.

The UN found in March 2025, for example, that the Israeli military had buried in a mass grave 15 emergency workers who it had picked off "one by one" after ambushing their vehicles.

The crews had been coming to the aid of another team attacked by the Israeli army earlier that day in Rafah. The UN noted that Israeli bulldozers had crushed the ambulances and then covered them with sand.

Similarly, Israel attacked and seized two large hospitals in Gaza, Nasser and al-Shifa, in early 2024. After its forces pulled out, large mass graves were found close by both.

At Nasser Hospital, three mass graves contained 392 bodies, including those of women, children, the elderly and injured people. Evidence was found of "field executions" and mutilations of some of the dead.

As with Myanmar, such atrocities by Israeli soldiers go uninvestigated and unpunished. Even after a video showed five reservists anally raping a Palestinian prisoner with a baton, causing him severe internal injuries, the Israeli military dropped all charges.

Also like Myanmar, Israel has let civilian groups from its Jewish population collude in its genocidal violence without punishment. Far-right groups have regularly been allowed to mass at crossing points to block the delivery of critically needed food. On repeated occasions, they have looted the aid.

In summer 2024, at the height of these blockades, it was found that three of the groups were being rewarded by Israel and the US with special tax-deductible status for donations.

Hypocrites to the end

In these and all other cases of suspected atrocities, Israel has refused access to outside investigators, just as it has journalists. It has continued that policy even after agreeing to a ceasefire in October 2025 - a ceasefire it has entirely ignored.

More than 1,670 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza during the ceasefire period.

Israel's aversion to transparency is likely to incriminate it further in the eyes of the ICJ's judges, just as it did for Myanmar.

The court has shown in its latest ruling that it is ready to fill evidential gaps, even if it means drawing on arm's-length investigations by UN agencies and international and local human rights bodies. There is a wealth of damning evidence already.

Gaza flooding is a catastrophe by design - and the spineless West is complicit
Read More »

The ICJ is also likely to accept the growing body of confessions made by Israeli soldiers of their involvement in atrocities and the systematic use of violence against the people of Gaza through AI, as set out by whistleblowing intelligence officers in a recent documentary, NAZA.

It is not just Israel, however, that has reasons to be fearful of the Myanmar judgment.

Several western states, including Britain, Canada, France and Germany, backed the genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ initiated by The Gambia. Separately, the US assessed in 2022 that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

On 19 November, Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, welcomed the ICJ ruling, ordered the expulsion of Myanmar's defence attache and threatened "further action". Four days later, Britain formally recognised the genocide and sanctioned five Myanmar generals.

The US noted that it had been the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response", and that it shared "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights" of the Rohingya.

Western states' hypocrisy is fully on show. They have failed in their duty to prevent an even more obvious genocide in Gaza than the one in Myanmar, despite the World Court warning them of the "plausible risk" in January 2024.

Not only that, but the genocide in Gaza would have been impossible without active help from the US, Britain and Germany in supplying the weapons used to kill Palestinians en masse, providing intelligence to Israel and offering diplomatic cover.

The case against Myanmar took seven years to reach its conclusion after The Gambia brought it to the ICJ. If a similar timeline is followed in Gaza's case, Israel may not be found guilty for another three or four years.

Israel can do a lot more damage to the enclave and its population in the meantime. The Myanmar case should prove to western states that they need to act now. It should galvanise a response.

Instead, hypocrites to the bitter end, western capitals will carry on backing the current genocide in Gaza as they lament the earlier one in Myanmar.

item.title: The epidemic we continue to tolerate. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Every year, November 25 is observed as the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Violence against women appears in a myriad of forms, ranging from wife abuse to rape, dowry killings, acid throwing, sexual harassment, and sexual slavery through international trafficking in women .
Violence against women has many causes, including patriarchal domination, forced marriage, gender stereotypes, lack of gender sensitivity, corruption in the judicial system, unequal power relations, unemployment, feminization of poverty, or trafficking of women.
In addition, low levels of education, low socio-economic status, younger age, alcohol abuse, childhood experience of abuse, witnessing violence between parents, lack of communication between partners, and living in communities with stronger norms of masculine dominance are among some of the determinants.
In different cultures around the world, socio-cultural norms deepen the subjugation of women. Societies press women to ensure abuse to protect family honour and the acceptance of male dominance. It contributes to normalization of domestic violence.
Violence against women is a global phenomenon that cuts across boundaries of age, socioeconomic status, education, and geography. Estimates by the World Health Organization (WHO) indicate that about 35% of women and girls worldwide have experienced physical and, or sexual intimate partner violence or non-partner sexual violence in their lifetime.
However, these numbers only tell a part of the story. Even when data is available, it is likely that the figures are an underestimate as it is notoriously difficult to collect sensitive information on violence against women, when the victims can fear coming forward or feel ashamed.
The impact of domestic violence is catastrophic, impairing the physical and psychological health of survivors, as well as their social and economic stability. Children who are witnesses to domestic violence are more likely to experience poor developmental outcomes and boys growing up in abusive households are likely to repeat the behaviours of their fathers in their own households when they grow up.
Even though various studies suggest that women in poor households are at a higher risk of domestic violence, the link between poverty and violence is poorly understood.
Violence against women also has an impact on the lives of many women beyond the direct victims. The fear of violence can prevent women from pursuing education, working, or exercising their political rights and voice.
In every region of the world, women consistently feel more insecure than men, although the levels of insecurity significantly vary across regions. Violence against women is not only a cause of gender inequality, it is also a consequence of it.
In many places, gender-based violence is reinforced by discriminatory laws and exclusionary social norms that undermine women and girls' opportunities for education, income, and independence. This accompanies shifting power relations within households and communities, especially when there is resentment against women who move away from conventional roles.
Detailed data from BBS suggests that adolescent girls, regardless of their marital status, continue to be vulnerable to all forms of violence. The hidden battle faced by victims of domestic violence is within the household -- they are isolated, without support or resources, suffering in silence, fearing further abuse or retribution, and are subject to shame and stigma which further inhibit them from seeking assistance or reporting abuses.
Globally, combating domestic violence requires a comprehensive strategy. It is essential to enhance legal protections for victims and ensure accountability for perpetrators. For all these, domestic violence laws must be enacted and enforced.
These will also involve improving police and judicial responsiveness, and guaranteeing violence victims access to legal aid and protection orders for survivors. Specific approaches and measures are needed for combatting increased domestic violence during shocks and vulnerabilities as seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
In order to break the cycle of abuse, it is essential to transform societal views on domestic violence. This can be done through public awareness campaigns, educational initiatives, and community programs. It is necessary to challenge the norms and beliefs that sustain domestic violence, fostering a culture where violence is unacceptable and survivors are supported and empowered.
Policy interventions should focus on the longer-term by changing discriminatory social norms, closing gender gaps or building awareness. Innovative and aggressive policy that aims to change outcomes (such as increasing women’s voice in the community) may change norms. Although norms should guide the design of culturally sensitive policies and programs, they should not constrain or undermine initiatives.
Enhancing support services for domestic violence survivors is critical. This involves creating safe shelters, offering counselling and healthcare, and providing economic empowerment programs to help survivors rebuild their lives.
Ensuring these services are accessible and meet the diverse needs of all survivors, regardless of their socio-economic background or location, is vital. And so much more effort is needed to tackle the patterns of violence that cut deep into many societies so that they are not perpetuated across generations.

Violence against women requires immediate and ongoing action. It demands a collective effort from the government, civil society, communities, and individuals to challenge the cultural and social norms enabling domestic violence, protect and support survivors, and hold perpetrators accountable.

item.title: Understanding the rise of divorce. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On a humid Tuesday morning, Rumana, 29, sits on a plastic chair outside a zonal office of the Dhaka South City Corporation, a brown envelope on her lap. Inside it is a notice that will end her seven-year marriage. She is a schoolteacher. Her husband stopped speaking to her months ago, except to remind her that his mother wanted a grandson and a larger share of her salary. Her parents once told her to be patient. This time, her father came with her.
Rumana is a composite, drawn from accounts reported in Bangladeshi newspapers, but her queue is real. In 2022, the two city corporations of Dhaka received 13,288 divorce applications, about 37 a day, or one every 40 minutes. Seven in 10 were filed by wives. Behind each envelope is a story Bangladesh has long preferred not to tell.
Bangladesh's crude divorce rate doubled in a single year, from 0.7 per 1,000 people in 2021 to 1.4 in 2022, according to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS). For 15 years before that, between 2006 and 2021, it had moved only between 0.6 and 1.1. The rate eased to 1.1 in 2023, but it is still well above where it stood before the pandemic.
The numbers also break a familiar assumption. Divorce is often treated as an urban, middle-class phenomenon, yet BBS found it is higher in villages: 1.1 per 1,000 in rural areas in 2023, against 0.9 in cities. Division by division, the gap is wide: Rajshahi recorded 2.2 per 1,000, while Dhaka division stood at 1.3.
In the capital, the city corporations count every notice. Dhaka North alone received 5,459 applications in 2024, and 5,305 of them became effective divorces. Reconciliation, which the law requires the authorities to attempt within 90 days, almost never works: In Dhaka North in 2022, only 128 couples, about 2%, settled their differences.
The most striking change is who signs the notice. In Dhaka, about 70% of divorce applications are filed by women; in Dhaka North, women filed 4,081 of 7,414 notices in 2021, and employed women topped the list. City officials describe a quiet shift at home as well: Parents who once sent daughters back to abusive in-laws now increasingly help them file to protect them.
The shift is not only urban. In a village in Rajshahi, the division with the country's highest divorce rate, a 23-year-old woman, married at 16 to a man who left for Saudi Arabia within a year, waits each month for remittances that stop coming and phone calls that grow shorter.
When she finally hears that he has married again abroad, she sends her divorce notice through the local kazi . Her story, too, is a composite, but it echoes a pattern officials describe across the north: Young brides, long absences, and marriages that exist mostly on paper.
The reasons people give are older than the trend. BBS's 2022 survey, which for the first time asked divorced people directly, found extramarital relationships to be the leading cause. Alongside it sit dowry demands, physical and mental abuse, interference from in-laws, and long separations as husbands migrate abroad for work.
More women now earn their own money, more have finished school, and a smartphone can connect a woman in a village to a lawyer, a hotline or a friend who left before her.
Early marriage makes many of these unions fragile from the start. BBS found that 40.9% of those who married in 2022 were under 18, and 6.5% were under 15. The average age at marriage was 18.8 years for women and 25.3 for men, a gap of more than six years. A girl married before she finishes school often enters a household where she has little voice, few skills to earn, and no say in the decisions that shape her life. When such marriages break, she has the least to fall back on.
There is a darker side too. Lawyers and rights groups report men who make life unbearable so that their wives will file first, in the belief that this frees them from paying denmohor , the dower promised at marriage. Even women's "choice" to leave can be coerced.
For Rumana, filing was the easy part. The harder part begins after the 90 days. A divorced woman in Bangladesh still meets whispers at weddings, landlords who hesitate to rent to her, and relatives who ask what she did wrong. Remarriage is rare: BBS figures cited by officials show that only about 4% of widowed or divorced people remarry.
Men are not spared either, though their losses are less often discussed. Many lose regular contact with their children, and few seek help for the shame or loneliness that follows, in a culture that expects them to stay silent. Counselling services that could support both partners are almost absent outside a handful of private clinics in Dhaka.
Children carry much of the weight. The country has no institutional system to track what happens to families after divorce, so no one can say how many children are affected or how they fare. That silence matters in a country where, according to Unicef, nearly 90% of children aged 1-14 already face physical or emotional punishment at home each month; family breakdown can raise that risk further.
The law has not kept pace. Muslim divorce is still governed by the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance of 1961. Custody follows rules shaped by religious personal law, maintenance is hard to enforce, and many women never receive their dower. Hindu women, under their own personal law, have no clear right to divorce at all.
It is tempting to read the rising numbers as proof that the family is collapsing. A better reading is that more Bangladeshis, mostly women, are refusing marriages that were already broken. A society cannot wish divorce away, but it can decide how much it costs.
Three steps would help.
First, count properly : A national register that links divorce records to the children involved would let the state see who needs support.
Second, make the 90-day reconciliation period real : This has to be done with trained counsellors rather than a notice from a zonal office, and with fast-track enforcement of dower and child maintenance when reconciliation fails.
Third, reform personal laws: Every woman, whatever her religion, must have a clear and equal right to leave a marriage and to keep her children safe. Schools, employers and mosques can also help by treating divorced women and their children as neighbours, not cautionary tales.
Mahmodul Hasan Shesheir (Research Associate, Yale University, USA). Jinat Tamanna (MPH student, North South University) and Iftekhar Alam (undergraduate student, Chittagong Veterinary and Animal Sciences University).

Our tourism sector has a friendliness problem. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On paper, the launch of a three-month tourism carnival in Cox's Bazar is a welcome initiative.
Featuring cultural performances, adventure activities, food festivals, beach sports, and family entertainment, the event reflects a recognition that tourism must be about experiences rather than merely destinations.
With that said, Bangladesh's tourism challenge has never been a lack of attractions.
From the world's longest natural sea beach to the Sundarbans, tea gardens, archaeological sites, hill tracts, rivers, and rich cultural heritage, Bangladesh has always possessed tourism assets. The problem is that possessing attractions and being a tourist-friendly destination are not the same thing.
What we have failed to recognize is the importance of the visitor experience itself. Tourists, whether domestic or international, need more than events and slogans. They need safety, cleanliness, reliable transportation, clear information, quality accommodation, and confidence that they can enjoy their trip without harassment, fraud, or unnecessary inconvenience.
Sadly, we have never quite been able to provide that.
This is especially important for women travellers and families. A destination cannot truly thrive if visitors constantly have to worry about personal security, overcrowding, poor waste management, or inadequate emergency services.
Tourism flourishes where people feel comfortable, welcomed, and protected. These should not be viewed as ancillary issues but rather as the foundation of any serious tourism strategy.
Bangladesh must move beyond treating tourism as a seasonal activity or a series of promotional events. It should be developed as a major economic sector capable of creating jobs, attracting investment, and improving the country's international image.
However, that will require sustained investment in infrastructure, training for service providers, environmental protection, law enforcement, and visitor-friendly governance.
Bangladesh’s tourism sector has long had the potential. But that will only be possible when we can provide a safe, clean, and welcoming environment.

item.title: The need to confront violence against women. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh has spent decades celebrating gains in girls' education, women's employment, and political representation. Yet behind these achievements lies a grim reality we all-too-often ignore: Violence against women remains one of the country's most pervasive and persistent injustices.
Progress cannot be measured solely by economic indicators when millions of women continue to face violence in their homes, workplaces, educational institutions, and online spaces.
This year's theme,"Speak out. Believe survivors. Demand justice," arrives at a moment when silence remains one of the greatest enablers of abuse.
Too often in our nation, public discussions focus on a survivor's conduct rather than a perpetrator's crime.
Too often, women are advised to be more careful instead of men being told to stop abusing.
Victim-blaming remains deeply embedded in our social fabric, discouraging reporting and shielding perpetrators from accountability. If we are to be taken seriously as a nation that is making progress, such regressive attitudes will simply not do.
The problem extends beyond social attitudes. Impunity remains a stubborn reality. Despite the countless documented cases of rape and domestic violence, that we continue to see such an alarming gap between legal protections and their enforcement is telling of how much work needs to be done on this front.
Bangladesh does not lack laws. What it lacks is consistent implementation, survivor-centred support services, timely investigations, and swift justice. Shelters, legal aid, counselling, and protection mechanisms remain inadequate for many women, especially those who need them most.
A nation with aspirations such as ours cannot tolerate a culture where violence against half its population is normalized and who are consistently questioned and doubted. Speaking out against misogyny, believing those who come forward, and demanding accountability from institutions is the bare minimum we can do.

item.title: Rohail Nazir's fifty books Asia Cup Rising Stars semi-finals spot for Pakistan Shaheens. [ dawn ]
item.description:
An unbeaten half-century by Rohail Nazir, followed by a devastating bowling display, helped Pakistan Shaheens defeat Nepal by 96 runs in their final Group ‘B’ match of the Asia Cup Rising Stars at the University of Doha for Science and Technology on Tuesday.

The defending champions remained unbeaten in the tournament, winning all three of their group matches to qualify for the semi-finals, where they will face Bangladesh A on Nov 27.

Batting first, Pakistan Shaheens were in trouble at 66-6 in 16.5 overs before wicket-keeper-batter Rohail steadied the innings with an unbeaten 64 off 83 balls, hitting four fours and three sixes.

After Hasan Nawaz fell for 28 off 59 balls, leaving the Shaheens at 88-7, Rohail added 70 runs for the eighth wicket with Ahmed Daniyal, who scored 16 off 35 balls, to help his side reach 168 before being bowled out in 42 overs.

For Nepal, Rashid Khan claimed five wickets for 39 runs, while Abhishesh Gautam took two.

Nepal’s chase got off to a disastrous start as Muhammad Imran and Mohammad Hasnain reduced them to 15-4 inside six overs. Hasnain struck twice in successive deliveries to dismiss Ishan Pandey and Lokesh Bam without scoring.

Left-arm spinner Sufyan Moqim then claimed three wickets as Nepal slumped to 59-9. Mayan Yadav offered some resistance with a top score of 41 off 50 balls but was trapped leg-before by Maaz Sadaqat as Nepal were dismissed for 72 in 17.3 overs.

Hasnain and Sufyan took three wickets each for 21 and 17 runs respectively, while Imran claimed two for 29.

Rohail was named player of the match for his match-winning innings.
