item.title: What are we failing to teach?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
“He who studies rides in cars and carriages.”
This familiar Bengali proverb is something many of us grew up hearing. It reflects a traditional understanding of education: S tudy hard, achieve good results, secure a good job, and build a prosperous life.
There is nothing wrong with that aspiration. Education should certainly provide children with the knowledge and skills they need to earn a living and improve their financial and material well-being.
But is that all education is meant to achieve?
Nearly 30 years ago, Une sco ’s Delors Report (1996) identified four broad purposes of education: “ L earning to know,” “learning to do,” “learning to be,” and “learning to live together.”
The first two concern knowledge and skills, while the latter two focus on developing the whole person and preparing young people for life with others.
In our education system, academic knowledge and examination performance naturally receive considerable attention. Yet in practice, “learning to be” and “learning to live together” often receive far less attention than academic achievement and job-related skills.
Are we educating students merely to pass examinations and acquire subject knowledge, or are we also helping them become confident, resilient, and emotionally healthy individuals who can understand others, navigate differences, build meaningful relationships and live well together?
Beyond the marks and grades
“Learning to be” is about becoming a complete human being, not simply a successful student. Education should help young people think independently, ask questions, communicate clearly, make thoughtful decisions, and reflect on their actions.
It should also nurture emotional intelligence, so they can understand their emotions, recognize different perspectives, respond with empathy, and build healthy relationships. Along the way, they need to develop confidence, resilience, integrity, and a sense of responsibility.
Yet these qualities can easily be overshadowed when educational success is measured mainly through marks, grades, examination results, and admission to prestigious institutions. Curiosity, creativity, empathy, and resilience may become secondary to the next examination or academic milestone.
Academic excellence matters. The concern arises when academic achievement becomes almost the sole measure of success. A student may achieve excellent grades and build a successful career while still struggling to handle failure, accept criticism and different opinions, acknowledge mistakes or work with people who are different.
That takes us to a deeper purpose of education. Beyond what students know and what they achieve, what kind of human beings are they becoming?
The answer cannot come only from what is prescribed in the curriculum or written in textbooks. It also depends on how children experience and engage with the world around them, how they interact with others, respond to differences, handle disagreements, and take responsibility for their actions. That is where “learning to live together” becomes equally important.
A child walks into a classroom carrying much more than a schoolbag. He or she carries a family background, social, and religious identity, hopes, fears, abilities, opportunities, and disadvantages. Yet once inside the classroom, all children are expected to learn together. The deeper question is whether we are also helping them learn how to live together.
This matters deeply in a socially diverse and economically unequal society such as Bangladesh. Children grow up with different levels of wealth, different beliefs, abilities, languages, family circumstances, and social experiences.
From an early age, they begin to notice who is respected, who is ignored, who is included, and who is left out. In this way, they begin to form ideas about fairness, often without being explicitly taught.
Discrimination does not always appear as open exclusion. It can take the form of a joke, a stereotype, a label, an unequal expectation or an assumption about what a child can achieve.
A child from a poorer family may be made to feel inferior. A child with a disability may be viewed as incapable rather than supported to participate. A child who is different from the majority may gradually feel that belonging is something to be earned rather than something everyone deserves.
Schools can either reinforce these attitudes or challenge them. A school that teaches equality but allows a child to be humiliated because of family circumstances sends a contradictory message. A school that speaks about inclusion but does not enable a child with a disability to participate fully does the same. Similarly, when academic competition dominates school life, children may learn to see one another more as rivals than as people with whom they can learn and grow.
This is why values cannot be taught only through lessons, definitions, or moral instruction. Children learn from what they experience.
A child who is listened to learns that his or her voice matters. A child who is treated with dignity learns what dignity means. A child who is allowed to make a mistake without humiliation learns that failure is part of learning. A child who sees others treated fairly begins to understand fairness not as an abstract principle, but as something that should guide everyday life.
The same is true of disagreement. Children will argue, compete, form friendships, and sometimes hurt one another. School can teach them that disagreement does not have to lead to hostility. Learning to live together does not mean teaching children to agree on everything. It means helping them learn how to disagree without hatred, humiliation, or exclusion.
Cooperation also has to be experienced, not simply encouraged. When children work together on projects, solve problems collectively, or take responsibility for shared activities, they learn to listen to different opinions, share responsibilities, and recognize the contribution of others. These are not activities outside education. They are part of what education should accomplish.
The purpose is not to make children identical in their beliefs, abilities or experiences. It is to help them understand that difference does not have to become division. In a diverse society, children need to learn how to live with people who may think differently, believe differently, or come from circumstances very different from their own.
Learning to live with nature
“Learning to live together” should extend beyond human relationships to our relationship with nature. Children need to experience that they are not separate from the natural world, but part of it, and that nature is not merely a resource for human use. It has its own value and deserves care and respect.
This understanding cannot come from textbooks alone. Children need opportunities to experience nature, observe living things, grow plants, understand water and waste, and see how human actions affect the world around them.
The aim is not simply to teach children about the environment, but to help them develop a sense of belonging to nature and responsibility towards it. To live well is not only to live well with one another, but to live with nature in a way that respects its right to exist and flourish.
Education for life
Education should prepare children not only for work, but for life; not only to compete, but to cooperate; and not only to succeed as individuals, but to live together as human beings.
Its real measure lies not only in what children know or achieve, but in who they become and how they treat others. Can they live meaningful lives, respect differences, respond to inequality, participate responsibly in society, and care for the world they share?
The question before us, therefore, is not simply what technical skills our children acquire, but what kind of people our education institutions are helping them become.
And ultimately, what kind of society will those people build?
Dr Somnath Saha is Assistant Professor, Brac IED, Brac University.

item.title: The government gets something right. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
It's easy enough -- and I do it often enough -- to point to something a government is doing wrong and then snarl about that thing the government is doing wrong. It is more difficult to find something a government is doing right and then congratulate that government.
It's possible to go on and say that this is because governments do so many things wrong and so few right -- but that would be cynical. I am indeed cynical, but at least part of this is that it's so much more fun to criticize than it is to praise.
Yet here we are, the Bangladeshi government is getting a good part of cleaning up the banking system right.
We all wish we weren't here in the first place of course. We'd all prefer that there weren't years and years where well connected people were able to pillage the banking system. Yet there were, and we've now got to deal with what did indeed happen.
What happened is that people borrowed money they had little ability to repay -- or little intention to repay. That causes a significant problem for the rest of us because stealing from banks is not victimless.
Too many loans not repaid means the bank will -- eventually -- run out of capital and fail.
If the banks fall over, then a basic requirement for a useful economy stops happening -- our savings stop being recycled into the investments that make the future richer. We do not want this to happen.
One part of this is to identify and isolate those banks that have lost some or all of their capital. This is being done : “15 banks, including five merged Shariah-based banks, were behind more than 85% of the over Tk600,000 crore in non-performing loans (NPLs).”
Some of the NPLs are just loans that didn't work. That always does happen and a system that had none at all would be a system that wasn't lending enough money -- thereby failing to make the future richer. But a large portion of these were loans that should never have been made -- to those who could not, or would not, repay them. People who were insiders at the banks and were able to short-circuit the normal lending standards.
So, now we know which banks have these problems. We can then use special measures to manage these banks. Insist that they raise more capital. Merge some of them. Keep a special eye on who they lend to. If necessary -- and we don't like doing this but sometimes we must -- put more tax money into the banks so they have capital again.
We also want to punish those who borrowed and did not repay. This is also being done : “A court in Chittagong on Thursday sentenced former land minister Saifuzzaman Chowdhury Javed to 15 years in prison for embezzling Tk25 crore in loans from United Commercial Bank Limited (UCBL) and laundering the money abroad.”
This is also good and the right thing to do. Thieves should go to jail and thieves who threaten the entire economic system with their thefts should spend more time in jail than those who steal lesser things.
We're never going to catch everyone who stole from the banks. But that's not actually the point. While it would be nice to punish them it's still not the point. It would be just to jail them all, but even that's not the point.
What we must do is make sure that no one steals from the banking system in the same way again. Because, as above, having a banking system is what makes the joint future richer. So we need to protect the banking system itself, not just some of the money in some of the banks.
Fifteen years -- plus a fine -- is a hefty sentence. The next man who decides he'd like to defraud a bank will think quite a lot about whether he's willing to risk it. Sure, it's great to fine as well and that might put some of the money stolen back into the bank.
The correct reaction to a banking system that has been pillaged is for the central bank -- and so the taxpayers -- to recapitalize the banks so that there is still a functional banking system.
This is needed to make the future richer. Then we need to visit those who stole all the money with prosecutions and long jail sentences so that no one tries this again.
The Bangladesh Bank, the government, is starting to do this. Good. We can be cynical and think that most governments don't do many good things. But that just makes praising the few done even more important. So, well done.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Restoring calm to the nation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The latest wave of arson, crude-bomb explosions, attacks on homes and public institutions, and road blockades across the country is terrorizing the nation, and as such, has veered away from mere political conflict into a direct assault on public safety, livelihoods, and the right of ordinary citizens to go about their lives without fear.
Such violence must be condemned unequivocally.
The incidents reported are alarming in both their scale and targets: Police stations torched, ancestral and present homes and businesses vandalized; vehicles set ablaze. These actions have resulted in the loss of lives, and if this is not senseless violence, then nothing is. These are not isolated incidents that can be brushed aside as routine political tension. They point to a dangerous erosion of public order that demands an immediate and decisive response.
There can simply be no justification for setting fire to buildings, hurling crude bombs, attacking police personnel, or targeting homes and businesses over their owners' political affiliations.
There should not be a need for editorials in newspapers to understand that political parties and their supporters should be refraining from using street violence and disruption as a shortcut to force political comebacks. It goes without saying that this is neither legitimate politics nor what ordinary citizens expect from those seeking public trust. Grievances must be pursued through peaceful channels, and those who organize, finance, or carry out attacks must be prosecuted, regardless of their political connections.
At the same time, resolving deep political friction requires genuine engagement: To that end, the government must consider keeping the door open to political dialogue. Having said that, it must, without fail, ensure that it never projects weakness or cedes the initiative to anarchic elements. This lax treatment of such incidents is partially the reason why mob violence has grown so rampant over the past couple of years.
Restoring order also requires empowering law enforcement agencies with a clear, unambiguous mandate to enforce the law and protect public life and national assets. When police stations, transport corridors, and private properties are repeatedly targeted across districts, reactive measures are no longer tenable. Intelligence gathering, preventive policing, and rapid intervention must be strengthened so citizens see an effective security strategy and can begin to feel more secure.
Firm enforcement must also remain rooted in the rule of law. A security crackdown cannot become a licence for arbitrary arrests or political profiling, something that we have also regrettably seen too much of in recent times.
Detaining individuals without credible evidence of specific offenses only deepens public mistrust and fuels instability. Arrests must be evidence-based, detainees' rights respected, and investigations conducted transparently and impartially so that every citizen - regardless of political affiliation - is assured equal protection.
People should not have to weigh the risk of a bomb blast or a burning vehicle before sending their children to school, commuting to work, or moving freely around their cities. If there is to be peace in the nation, the government must demonstrate both political maturity and state resolve: Meaningful dialogue paired with decisive, lawful policing, clear accountability, and a zero-tolerance stance toward political violence.
Our nation cannot and must not be left at the mercy of those looking to destabilize it.

item.title: Beyond the law: Rethinking human rights through the social sciences. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On an ordinary day in Kalyanpur in May this year, Md Russel was allegedly abducted by 20 to 25 men after refusing a Tk15,000 monthly extortion demand. They took him into a slum and beat him until locals heard his cries and intervened. Two days later, he filed a police complaint. But instead of investigating, police reportedly urged him to settle the matter with the accused.
For Russel, filing a complaint did not lead to an investigation. His experience raises questions about police discretion and whether people can seek justice without being pressured by those they accused. This one incident cannot represent the entire justice system, but it shows how institutional practices affect people’s ability to exercise their rights.
Like many stories across Bangladesh, this reminds us that human rights violations are not abstract. They are lived, contested, and silenced at the intersection of class, gender, and power.
Understanding human rights requires more than knowing what the law guarantees. We must understand why some can claim those rights while others cannot.
We speak of human rights in legal terms. The Constitution guarantees equality of all before the law, freedom of speech, and protection against arbitrary arrest. Bangladesh is a signatory to major human rights treaties. Rights are framed as legal entitlements to be claimed, defended, or litigated.
Yet, law can tell us what rights exist, but not why some exercise them more easily than others.
Legal anthropologist Sally Engle Merry showed how human rights are reshaped as they move across societies and institutions . Rights acquire meaning through local contexts, social relations, and everyday practices. To understand whether rights are protected, we must look beyond legal documents to see how individuals exercise them.
In the Chittagong Hill Tracts, indigenous communities see land not as property but as ancestral identity. When the state applies land laws designed for flatland ownership, it challenges these cultural meanings.
As Signe Leth of the International Work Group for Indigenous Affairs notes, land is not just a commodity for Indigenous Peoples but a part of their identity, spirituality, and life.
The same gap appears in the experience of the hijra community. Recognition as a third gender in 2013 did not automatically remove the stigma and exclusion that shape access to housing, education, healthcare, and employment.
Changing the law and changing social relations are not the same thing. These examples show how culture and social norms shape rights, a concern central to Anthropology.
Garment workers’ experiences show how workplace hierarchy, gender, and class affect the ability to claim rights. Despite the Labour Act's protections, a 2025 study of 332 female garment workers found that 22$ of workers reported frequent sexual harassment inside the factories during the preceding six months by supervisors, male co-workers, and security guards.
For workers who depend on their wages, fear of job loss and retaliation can make formal protection difficult to claim. Applying a sociological lens shows that while a right may be guaranteed by law, whether someone can exercise it depends on their social circumstances.
Human rights also depend on institutions capable of enforcing the laws. A UN fact-finding report on the July-August 2024 violence in Bangladesh documented how weak internal oversight and barriers to prosecuting public officials hindered accountability. When complaints are handled by institutions implicated in abuses, victims may have little assurance of independent investigation or meaningful redress.
Finally, understanding human rights requires looking at the material conditions of freedom. When a child in a coastal village loses access to school due to flooding, or when a family is displaced by river erosion and cannot recover their livelihood, the problem is not just environmental or economic. It affects their ability to exercise basic rights.
A BIGD study of social assistance in Satkhira found that beneficiary selection could be shaped by kinship networks, political affiliation, gender, religious identity, and proximity to local representatives, despite formal eligibility criteria.
Economic vulnerability can also make travel, paperwork, legal support, and time away from work difficult to afford. Amartya Sen’s capability approach reminds us that freedom is not merely possessing a right, but having the real opportunity to use it.
Across these examples, rights are shaped by more than laws. They are shaped by the institutions people encounter, social hierarchies they live within, and the resources available to them.
If law is the pillar of rights, social science is its foundation. Each discipline offers a lens: Law defines rights and duties, anthropology reveals cultural meanings, sociology exposes inequality and social hierarchy, political science examines institutions and power, and development economics shows how material conditions affect freedom. Together, they reveal what a strictly legal lens cannot explain.
Bangladesh has made progress, from women’s participation to digital access. Yet persistent inequalities, gender-based violence, institutional weakness, and social exclusion remind us that rights cannot be legislated into existence. They must be supported by social and institutional change.
That includes complaint and redress mechanisms that protect complainants, stronger institutional oversight, and fewer financial and social barriers for marginalized groups.
Interdisciplinary research can strengthen rights protection by showing where rights on paper fail in practice and by involving affected communities in judging whether reform works.
Sanjid Tahsin Rakin is a research associate at the Brac Institute of Governance and Development (BIGD), Brac University.

item.title: How many must burn?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As of writing this editorial, five people -- including a nine-year-old girl and a fifteen-year-old boy -- are at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery after suffering severe respiratory tract burns in a Thursday night fire at a warehouse in Dhaka’s Mirpur-10.
That we continue to have warehouses packed with highly flammable material inside a residential structure in a densely populated neighborhood speaks volumes about chronic regulatory failure.
For years, Dhaka’s residential areas -- from Old Dhaka to Mirpur -- have been turned into ticking time bombs by illegal commercial storage, chemical depots, and unregulated workshops operating right beneath sleeping families.
Every single inferno follows the exact same tragic script: An avoidable blaze breaks out, innocent workers and children suffer horrific injuries or death, authorities express routine shock, and within days, regulatory enforcement returns to its usual slumber.
The presence of minors among the critically injured also raises urgent questions regarding child labour and basic workplace safety compliance. Storing mounds of combustible garment scraps without adequate ventilation, fire exits, or suppression equipment must be called what it is: Criminal negligence.
The responsibility for this recurring nightmare lies with relevant authorities such as RAJUK, who over the years have continued to display a level of disregard that simultaneously deserves scrutiny. Laws governing zoning, building codes, and hazardous storage exist on paper, yet they are rendered meaningless by weak oversight, bureaucratic inertia, and corruption that allow illegal warehouses to thrive unchecked in residential zones.
We must abandon this reactive, post-tragedy posture and launch an immediate, uncompromising eviction and inspection drive across Dhaka’s residential neighborhoods. Illegal commercial warehouses and flammable storage facilities must be sealed immediately, building owners and operators held criminally liable for safety violations, and strict zoning boundaries enforced without exception.
Citizens should not have to live in constant fear of being burned alive because regulators refuse to do their jobs.

item.title: The Rooppur reactor is ours. The fuel cycle isn't. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, at 3:16 PM, a controlled chain reaction on the bank of the Padma pushed 350 megawatts into the national grid.
Fifty years of waiting ended in a control room full of engineers who had probably stopped believing they would live to see it. Whatever else is true about Rooppur, that moment belongs to them, and to the country that paid for it.
What is happening to the bill for that moment is another matter.
The Tk26,181 crore increase in the project's cost is real, and it is almost entirely a currency story. The Russian credit was denominated in dollars at a projected Tk80; the rate is now Tk 122.40, and the taka lost more than 30% of its value after 2022.
Anyone presenting that arithmetic as a corruption story either cannot do the sum or is counting on you not doing it. The post-August 5 regime has been counting. 16 months into a mandate built on accountability, it has an Anti-Corruption Commission file alleging Tk590 billion in embezzlement, a figure repeated until it sounds like a finding, and no charge sheet a court has tested.
Rosatom denies the allegations and says procurement followed both countries' laws. Let that argument run its course. What cannot wait is the thing nobody is shouting about.
A reactor that runs is not a country that chooses. In October, five months after the first fuel assemblies went into the core, Dhaka signed a five-page memorandum with Washington on nuclear cooperation. It is non-binding. It creates no obligations. A document that obligates nobody is not a framework, it is a photograph of an intention.
Read it next to February's trade agreement and the picture sharpens. Bangladesh got its tariff cut, from 20% to 19%, worth roughly $85m a year on current export volumes. In exchange, the text commits Dhaka not to buy reactors, fuel rods, or enriched uranium from any country that jeopardizes essential US interests, with a narrow exception where an existing reactor has no alternative supplier. Article 4.3 lets Washington terminate the whole arrangement if Bangladesh enters a preferential trading relationship with a non-market economy.
Rooppur runs a Russian VVER-1200. Western reactors use different geometries and enrichment specifications, and conversion is economically prohibitive.
Every 12-18 months the core needs fresh fuel, and that fuel comes from Russia. The first reload falls due in 2027 or 2028. No clause in any of these documents hands Washington a veto tomorrow. What it hands Washington is a date, a supplier constraint, and a legal instrument, all timed to the moment our reactor becomes dependent and our leverage disappears. We did not sell a veto. We leased one.
The global order is fracturing, and middle powers are learning to work the fracture. The Hedgers , published by Cambridge in March, describes the method: Take what each power offers, concede in communiqués, never concede in contracts.
India is the model. It buys discounted Russian crude, keeps Russian spares flowing, deepens semiconductor and defense-technology ties with Washington, and gives ground in language it can withdraw later.
Bangladesh did the opposite, and did it in all three directions at once. Russian fuel, Chinese payment plumbing, American permission. We called it balancing. It was stacking: Three dependencies laid on top of each other until the whole structure rested on nothing that was ours.
Even the payment workaround is failing. CIPS was supposed to let us settle with Moscow in yuan. It has not. Banks in Dhaka and in China have both flinched at the sanctions exposure, instalments sit in a Sonali Bank account that cannot be moved, and Moscow now talks about rupees and a Russian bank branch in the capital. The plumbing exists on paper and jams in practice, which is what happens when you build a bypass out of other people's infrastructure.
Washington has done this before, and closer to home. In 1971 it sailed the USS Enterprise into the Bay of Bengal for no reason a Bangladeshi needs explained. Financial architecture is simply the quieter version of the same gesture.
None of this is a case for abandoning Rooppur, and it is certainly not a case for defaulting on the IMF. It is a case for spending the next 18 months differently.
Start with Moscow, where we have more leverage than we use. The delays hurt Rosatom too, and Russia has already waived penalties on the project and pushed the first principal repayment back to September 2028, which is not the behaviour of a creditor with no stake in keeping the reactor alive.
Dhaka should be asking now, formally and publicly, for a longer grace period and a restructuring of the repayment curve, and should ask as a partner with a working reactor rather than as a supplicant with a problem.
Then capture what the plant actually earns. Fully operational, Rooppur displaces billions of dollars of imported LNG and furnace oil every year. That is foreign exchange that currently vanishes into the fuel bill and will now stay home.
It should not be absorbed into general revenue and spent. It should be ring-fenced into a debt-servicing fund with statutory protection, so that the plant pays for itself and builds the buffer we will need the first time the taka slips again.
And diversify the balance sheet before the reload window closes. Bangladesh has been a shareholder in the New Development Bank since 2021 and has drawn on it; the bank is targeting $30bn of approvals across 2022 to 2026, with a rising share in local currencies.
Partner status in the BRICS architecture should be a standing diplomatic ask rather than an occasional communiqué line, and local-currency settlement with India and China should move from aspiration to agreement. India's caution about expansion is a real constraint. It is not a reason to stop asking.
This reactor will light homes for 60 years. We waited half a century for it, borrowed to build it, and are now being asked to trade the keys to its fuel cycle for a tariff cut that rounds to nothing.
The current is flowing. The country is not yet in the control room.
Zakir Kibria is a Bangladeshi writer, policy analyst, and entrepreneur based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

item.title: Justice for the Rohingya. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We are pleased to see that nearly a decade after Myanmar's brutal military crackdown in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has delivered a landmark judgment, finding Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya community.
For the Rohingya, this has been a long and painful wait, and while it is undoubtedly a historic decision, it's also one that must lead to more than international condemnation.
The atrocities are not unknown: Thousands of Rohingya civilians were killed or subjected to widespread sexual violence and extreme brutality, and entire villages were destroyed.
These were not isolated incidents of violence. They were part of a systematic campaign against a vulnerable ethnic minority whose very existence was repeatedly denied.
For Bangladesh, this judgment carries particular significance. We have borne an enormous humanitarian and economic responsibility by sheltering more than a million Rohingya refugees for years despite stretched resources, yet the prospect of safe repatriation continues to look distant.
Bangladesh cannot be expected to shoulder this responsibility indefinitely while Myanmar evades accountability.
The ruling must now be followed by meaningful international action. The ICJ has called on Myanmar to facilitate the safe return of refugees and make reparations to victims. However, a court judgment alone cannot guarantee either.
The international community must now do its part to put pressure on Myanmar's military leadership, demand cooperation with investigations, and ensure that those responsible face consequences. Regional powers must also stop treating the crisis as a diplomatic inconvenience.
Repatriation must also be handled with care. Rohingya refugees cannot be sent back into the same conditions that forced them to flee. Their safety, citizenship rights, freedom of movement, and dignity must be guaranteed.
For too long, the Rohingya have been denied justice, identity and a place to call home. This judgment is an important step towards accountability; now the world must ensure it is not also the end of the effort.

item.title: Pakistan cruise to eight-wicket win over Sri Lanka to seal Test series 1-0. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Pakistan wrapped up an eight-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second and final Test, chasing down a target of 90 in just 13 overs to seal the two-match series 1-0 on Friday.

The hosts needed only 90 minutes on the fourth morning to complete the job after Mohammad Abbas dismissed the last Sri Lankan batter to end the visitors’ second innings at 316.

It was Pakistan’s first Test win since they beat the West Indies in the summer and their first series victory in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle.

The result was also just their third win in 11 matches in the current cycle, following draws against South Africa and the West Indies and series defeats in Bangladesh and England.

The first Test against Sri Lanka, also played in Rawalpindi, had ended in a draw.

Sri Lanka, who had resumed at 309-9, added seven runs before Asitha Fernando was trapped lbw for two by Abbas. Fernando reviewed the decision, but ball-tracking showed the delivery clipping the top of middle stump.

Abbas finished with three wickets for 55 runs from 34 overs, including 15 maidens. Aamer Jamal also claimed three wickets for 67, while Razaullah took two for 116 and Saqib Khan one before being sidelined by a hamstring injury.

Sri Lanka’s total left Pakistan needing 90 for victory, with Milan Rathnayaka unbeaten on 66 from 88 balls, including 12 fours.

His fighting innings had been central to a recovery after the visitors were dismissed for 98 in their first innings and conceded a 227-run lead when Pakistan replied with 325.

Pakistan’s pace attack had made full use of a green-tinged pitch to bowl Sri Lanka out cheaply on the opening day and put the hosts firmly in control.

The tourists began their second innings 153 runs behind and slipped to 10-2, but half-centuries from Kusal Mendis (53), Sonal Dinusha (54) and Rathnayaka helped them reach 316 and avoid an innings defeat.

Their 235-run effort on the third day briefly revived the contest, although the eventual target remained modest.

Pakistan began the chase positively, with Azan Awais and Tayyab Arif putting on 18 for the opening wicket. The stand ended when Lahiru Kumara bowled Tayyab for 13, with the batter beaten by movement off the pitch after striking three fours.

Azan was joined by Mohammad Taha, but the latter’s stay was brief. Asitha Fernando trapped him lbw for four, and Taha’s review failed as the ball was shown to be clipping leg stump. Pakistan were 37-2, but Sri Lanka could not build on the breakthrough.

Aamer was promoted up the order and turned the chase into a brisk finish. He struck 34 not out from 22 balls, hitting five fours and a six, and added an unbroken 53 with Azan for the third wicket.

Aamer attacked from the outset, taking boundaries off Fernando and Kumara before finishing the match with a four off Prabath Jayasuriya. Azan remained unbeaten on 32 from 36 balls, with five fours, as Pakistan reached 90-2 in 13 overs.

item.title: A better world for children. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
With November 20 being the anniversary of the adoption of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, this day serves as both a celebration of young potential and a sobering audit of global conscience.
Across the globe, millions of children are growing up amid armed conflict, climate displacement, and deepening economic inequality, trapped in crises engineered by adults.
In our own country, tens of millions of young citizens represent the very foundation of our nation's demographic future, yet face relentless threats to their safety, education, and well-being.
While we have made commendable strides over the decades in reducing infant mortality and expanding school enrollment, grave structural failures have continued to rob our children of a secure, peaceful upbringing.
At present, persistent inflation and economic strain have forced vulnerable families into desperate measures, fueling a troubling resurgence of child labour in hazardous informal sectors and early marriages that cut short the futures of young girls.
Meanwhile, climate-induced disasters routinely displace families, disrupting schooling and exposing children to malnutrition and preventable diseases.
Even within spaces meant to nurture them, our children are far from safe. Chronic teacher shortages, under-resourced classrooms, and an unforgiving, grade-obsessed academic culture have created an environment of acute psychological distress.
All of this is compounded by reckless traffic, pollution, and the now normalization of violence, all of which contribute to threatening young lives daily.
Commemorating this day cannot remain an exercise in ceremonial speeches and hollow pledges. A peaceful, thriving future for Bangladesh is impossible unless the adults in this country begin to treat children’s rights with the urgency they demand.
Investing in a safe, equitable, and peaceful world for our children is our highest moral and national duty.

item.title: Breaking the cycle of cronyism. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The recent assessment by The Economist, which has issued a stark warning that Bangladesh’s decades-long economic success story risks unravelling under the weight of a banking sector teetering on the edge of insolvency, must be taken seriously.
That non-performing loans (NPLs) have been allowed to climb to 33%, when neighbours India and Pakistan sit on 1.7% and 5% respectively, tells us everything we need to know about the state of the finance sector and what has been done to it over the past two decades.
The all-too-predictable result is a stagnant economy where private-sector credit growth is down to a 33-year low and GDP growth projections at 3.7%. What is most concerning, however, is the increase in poverty rate for a third consecutive year.
As The Economist points out, much of this crisis stems from years of kleptocratic lending and politically connected capture -- particularly within state-owned and Islamic banks, where massive sums were funnelled to favoured conglomerates.
Yet, if we are to reverse this trajectory, and reverse it we must for the future of this nation, diagnosing past abuses is insufficient.
We must confront the deeply entrenched political habits that persist even today, raising serious fears that the present practice of restructuring troubled banks could merely become a vehicle to reward a new set of cronies.
Early policy measures have sparked debate over how best to balance recovery with discipline. Shielding distressed borrowers and printing money only risks the economy more and delays the tough structural reforms that have been needed for years.
Rewriting this grim narrative requires an uncompromising, collective commitment across the state, regulators, and the private sector. It starts with insulating financial institutions from political patronage. Simultaneously, businesses, civil society, and lawmakers must rally behind transparent governance and fiscal discipline.
Bangladesh’s economic resilience was built by millions of hardworking citizens; safeguarding it only happens if we successfully break this toxic cycle of crony capitalism.

item.title: When we stop treating children like children. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is a familiar joke in South Asian families. A relative gives a child money as Eidi on Eid. The child is happy, counts the notes, and starts thinking about what to buy. Then comes the familiar instruction: “Give it to me. I will keep it safe for you.” And somehow, the money disappears.
We laugh about this tradition when it appears in memes. But have we considered what it teaches children about ownership and trust?
The issue is not a few hundred or a thousand taka. It is whether we recognize that the money belongs to the child.
I have tried to handle this differently with my own daughter. Whenever she receives money, I save it and maintain an Excel sheet recording who gave it, when, and how much. She can see the record. The money remains hers; my responsibility is to keep it safe until she is ready to use it. I want her to understand that money has value and that she can trust me to respect what belongs to her.
This small example reflects a much bigger issue in our parenting culture. Much of South Asian parenting developed in circumstances very different from those in which our children are growing up. Our parents and grandparents often faced economic insecurity and limited opportunities. Saving every taka, prioritizing education, and maintaining strict discipline were understandable responses to those challenges. But circumstances change, while traditions often remain.
We tell children to study hard because we have sacrificed everything for them. We expect them to listen to their elders without questioning them. We remind them of how much we have done for them and worry about what people will say if they make choices we disagree with.
Usually, there is love behind these expectations. Parents want their children to have better lives. The problem begins when protection becomes control, sacrifice becomes emotional debt, and respect becomes unquestioning obedience.
We want independent children, yet we often make almost every decision for them, from what they wear and whom they befriend to what they study and which career they pursue. Then we wonder why they struggle to make decisions on their own.
Independence does not suddenly develop at 18 or 25. Children learn it through everyday experiences. They need opportunities to make choices, take responsibility, make mistakes, and learn from the consequences.
Of course, young children need guidance. A six-year-old may not understand the importance of saving money. But guidance is not the same as ownership. We can help children manage their money without taking it away or deciding how it should be spent. If they are too young to keep it safely, we can save it on their behalf and explain what we are doing.
The same principle applies to other aspects of their lives. Children need to know that their opinions matter and that asking questions does not automatically make them disrespectful.
Our understanding of discipline also deserves reflection. We often hear adults say, “I was beaten as a child, and I turned out fine.” But surviving an experience does not mean it was good for us, nor does it mean we should repeat it with the next generation.
Children need boundaries and guidance, but these do not have to come through fear, humiliation, or physical punishment.
The world our children will inherit will demand more than obedience. Artificial intelligence is changing work, information is everywhere, and careers are becoming less predictable.
Children will need critical thinking, financial awareness, emotional maturity, and the confidence to make decisions independently. We cannot prepare them for an uncertain future if we discourage them from questioning adults or making choices for themselves.
A child can respect a parent and still disagree. A teenager can love their family and still ask why a particular rule exists. An adult child can be grateful for their parents' sacrifices without surrendering every personal decision. Gratitude should not become a lifelong obligation to fulfil someone else's expectations.
Children’s rights are not limited to laws and policies. They are reflected in ordinary moments at home: When we listen instead of dismissing them, apologize when we are wrong, allow them to express disagreement and give them age-appropriate responsibility.
This does not mean letting children do whatever they want. It means gradually moving from making every decision for them to helping them make decisions for themselves.
Perhaps the next time a child receives Eidi , we can simply ask: “It is your money. What would you like to do with it?” They may spend it on something we consider unnecessary. They may save it and later change their minds. That is part of learning.
On World Children’s Day, perhaps we should ask ourselves whether we are only providing for our children or also preparing them to live independently. Our children will eventually face situations for which we have no ready answers.
We cannot prepare them for that world by controlling every step they take. We need to give them enough guidance to make thoughtful decisions, enough freedom to learn from mistakes, and enough security to know that they can always come home for support.
The real measure of parenting is whether they eventually develop the confidence to make their own decisions and the maturity to take responsibility for them. To raise independent children, we must learn to let go of control without letting go of care.
Iffat Naomee is an assistant professor at the Institute of Education and Research (IER), University of Dhaka. She specializes in curriculum, pedagogy, and EdTech.

item.title: Criminalize medical referral commissions now. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council’s (BMDC) code of professional conduct, etiquette, and ethics explicitly and unequivocally bars doctors from accepting commissions in exchange for referring patients to healthcare facilities.
A referral commission -- often called fee-splitting or “cut practice” -- is a financial arrangement in which a hospital, diagnostic centre, pharmacy, or specialist pays a kickback or a percentage of patient fees to a doctor, broker, or healthcare worker for referring patients to their facility.
The relevant clause in the BMDC code leaves no room for ambiguity:
“A doctor shall not offer to, or accept from, any person or organization (including diagnostic laboratories, hospitals, nursing homes, health centers, beauty centres or similar institutions) any financial or other inducement (including free or subsidized consulting premises or secretarial support) for referral of patients for consultation, investigation or treatment.”
Yet anyone who has sought medical treatment in this country knows how pervasive this practice has become, regardless of what the code says. We are all victims of an unethical system that inflates our medical bills.
In its biennial report (2025-2026), published this past week, Bangladesh Health Watch estimated that these kickbacks exceed Tk5 crore every single day. The report states:
“Based on conservative assumptions regarding patient volumes in major diagnostic centres, the authors estimate that commission payments may amount to approximately [Tk]5.1 crore each day, equivalent to [Tk]1,861 crore annually among the country's largest diagnostic providers alone. Although these estimates require independent validation, they highlight the potentially enormous scale of financial resources diverted through commission-based referral practices.”
Put in plain terms, patients bear a Tk1,861 crore burden every year -- not for medicines, treatments, or consultation fees, but simply to sustain an unethical alliance between doctors and diagnostic labs.
In a country where households finance roughly 73% of total health expenditure out of pocket -- one of the highest rates in the world -- and where a single serious illness can push a poor family into extreme poverty, why is this not a punishable offense?
The mechanism is straightforward: Physicians direct patients to specific pathology labs or imaging centres and pocket a fixed cut -- often 20% to 50% of the test fee -- in return.
Medical ethics codes globally, including those set by the World Medical Association, prohibit fee-splitting because financial incentives can bias clinical judgment, leading to unnecessary tests, repeated diagnostics, and inflated costs.
Despite the BMDC’s clear rules, diagnostic referral commissions remain largely unregulated and are not explicitly criminalized under statutory law, unlike in many other jurisdictions.
Many countries enforce strict statutory bans on healthcare kickbacks. For example, the United States enforces the federal Anti-Kickback Statute, while India’s National Medical Commission explicitly penalizes doctors caught taking referral commissions, including through the suspension of their licenses.
Health sector watchdogs such as Bangladesh Health Watch have repeatedly called for legal amendments to introduce direct criminal and financial penalties for this practice, but to no avail.
Worse still, the practice has recently gained institutional cover, allowing a section of senior public-sector physicians to profit unlawfully. A parliamentary standing committee recently found that Bangladesh Medical University (BMU) -- formerly BSMMU and commonly known as PG Hospital -- allowed specialist doctors to take a 30% commission on the gross income rather than the net profit from diagnostic tests, in violation of government rules.
Following a government audit, Parliament's Public Accounts Committee took up the issue and ordered the university to recover the excess payouts. Under existing rules, if a test generates Tk100 in revenue against Tk90 in costs, BMU specialists are entitled to 30% of the Tk10 profit. Instead, they have been taking 30% of the entire Tk100 proceeds -- a gross violation.
This scandal raises a fundamental question: Why does a 30% commission privilege exist at all when the national medical ethics code strictly prohibits such inducements
While it is unclear exactly when BMU introduced this provision, such revenue-sharing models were established under internal guidelines and Health Ministry frameworks -- typically tied to institutional evening practice -- to incentivize senior specialists to work within public facilities rather than refer patients to outside private clinics.
This raises another critical concern: Does allowing doctors at public hospitals to profit from referral commissions act as de facto encouragement for private practitioners to do the same, regardless of industry ethics and codes?
When public hospitals permit this practice, the government's health administration loses the moral authority to hold private practitioners accountable for accepting referral fees.
Indeed, fee-splitting appears to have become pervasive in recent years. With state-run grassroots health facilities suffering from doctor shortages and absenteeism, patients at the upazila level often have to rely on private hospitals and clinics.
Doctors at these private facilities routinely refer patients for X-rays, imaging, and lab tests to preferred diagnostic centres, profiting from hefty commissions at the expense of low-income rural and semi-urban families.
Patients at the sub-district level remain severely underserved by public medical facilities. The state minister for health's acknowledgement in parliament this past week offers a glaring example: Nearly half of all physician posts at upazila health complexes are vacant (6,288 out of 13,036 positions), alongside 21,656 vacancies among 57,306 class-three healthcare worker and staff posts.
In a fiscal year when the government justifiably boasts of substantially increasing the overall health budget for the first time in years, a pressing question remains: How will this increased outlay actually relieve the burden on poor patients?
Their limited funds continue to be drained by doctors' “cut practices,” inadequate services at understaffed government hospitals, and high treatment and medicine costs.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial. [ theguardian ]
item.description:
A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support

The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another.

This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives.

item.title: Combating the threat of cyber fraud. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
As Bangladesh's economy becomes increasingly reliant on digital communication and financial transactions, the risks of cyber fraud are growing alongside it. Bangladesh Bank's latest directive asking banks to raise awareness among exporters about cyber threats is, therefore, a welcome step.
However, awareness alone will not be enough unless it is accompanied by stronger safeguards, accountability, and a more comprehensive approach to cybersecurity.
The central bank's warning highlights a particularly concerning threat: The manipulation of export documents and fraudulent changes to payment instructions. Such schemes can result in substantial financial losses, damage business relationships, and undermine confidence in Bangladesh's export sector.
With international trade increasingly dependent on electronic exchanges of information, even a seemingly minor lapse in communication security can have serious consequences.
The recommended precautions -- including independently verifying changes to banking details, avoiding suspicious links, and reporting suspected fraud promptly -- are practical measures that exporters must take seriously. Banks, meanwhile, have a responsibility to ensure that these warnings reach businesses of all sizes, particularly smaller exporters who may lack dedicated IT and cybersecurity teams.
But we must also recognize that cybercrime is not limited to export transactions. From online banking scams and identity theft to phishing attempts and the theft of personal financial information, ordinary citizens are increasingly exposed to digital threats.
Protecting the country's financial ecosystem requires a coordinated effort involving banks, regulators, law enforcement agencies, and technology providers.
Bangladesh Bank must ensure that its directive translates into meaningful action. Banks should invest in stronger security systems, regular staff training, effective fraud detection mechanisms, and accessible reporting channels. There must also be clear procedures for responding to cyber incidents and helping affected customers.
As we move towards a more digitally connected economy, cybersecurity cannot remain an afterthought. The cost of prevention is far lower than the financial and reputational damage caused by fraud, and we must build institutions capable of ensuring cybersecurity for our people and businesses.

item.title: Getting the nation under control. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The spread of arson attacks, crude bomb explosions, and political violence across Bangladesh is rapidly becoming a dangerous reality, and should serve as a serious warning to the authorities.
What began as a troubling pattern of incidents in Dhaka has now spread to other districts, with attacks on police stations, political leaders' homes, and vehicles. Most alarmingly, the violence in Faridpur claimed the life of a Krishak Dal leader who suffered severe burns.
This is a deeply disturbing situation that warrants nothing short of immediate and aggressive intervention.
The authorities need to recognize the urgency of getting the country under control before the situation deteriorates further. When people begin questioning whether they can safely travel, send their children to school, or go about their daily lives, it is clear that public confidence in security is being eroded.
The government must act on several fronts: Law enforcement agencies need to strengthen intelligence gathering, increase surveillance in vulnerable areas, and identify those organizing and financing these attacks.
Perpetrators must be brought to justice swiftly, but investigations must remain evidence-based. Political affiliations cannot become an excuse for selective enforcement, nor should innocent people become victims of indiscriminate action.
Political parties, too, must understand their responsibility. Provocative statements, threats, and attempts to mobilize supporters through intimidation will only deepen instability. No political objective can justify violence or the destruction of public and private property.
Bangladesh has already endured too much political turmoil to allow another prolonged period of insecurity to take hold. The government cannot afford to wait for the situation to spiral further before responding with the seriousness it deserves.
Restoring law and order is not a task that can be postponed or delegated to political parties; it is a fundamental responsibility of the state, and the authorities must demonstrate, urgently, that they remain firmly in control.

item.title: China's used phones find new homes from Karachi to Algiers. [ dawn ]
item.description:
In the maze of Shenzhen’s neon-lit Huaqiangbei electronics market, buyers from Africa to Bangladesh buy dozens of used phones at a time — even with cracked screens — to sell back home.

“From all China, the broken mobile phones come here,” Akhtar Muhammad, 38, a Pakistani businessman, told AFP as he browsed the stacks of devices in the southern Chinese city.

“We will fix them in Pakistan.” The supply is mind-boggling. As the world’s largest smartphone producer, China discards over 400 million devices annually, the China Association of Circular Economy estimates.

As chip shortages and rising prices around the world make new devices harder to afford, the demand for pre-owned phones is also soaring.

Mama, a 24-year-old Nigerian buyer, said he had bought around 40 used phones in one day in Shenzhen, which this week hosts Asia-Pacific leaders including US President Donald Trump.

“They are more expensive in Africa because we don’t have big suppliers or markets like this one,” Mama told AFP. “If I buy and send them to my country, I get profit.” Nearby, another Nigerian buyer haggled with a stall owner. His haul included damaged iPhone 13 Pro and 14 Pro models bought for 1,000 to 2,000 yuan ($150 to $300) each.

He plans to repair their screens locally before shipping them home for a lucrative resale.

Repair not replace

In particular, people in emerging markets such as South Asia and Africa, where there is less purchasing power, are turning to used models, Counterpoint Research analyst Ivan Lam told AFP.

The global secondary smartphone market grew 13 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 150 million units, according to Counterpoint.

In Pakistan, people often opt to repair rather than replace broken devices, said Muhammad, who has been coming to China since 2007.

“Maybe people use one mobile phone for four or five years. It’s not the same like USA, Europe. They change every year or every six months,” he said.

But outside Huaqiangbei’s crowded stalls, a more formalised alternative is taking root: PaiJiTang Mall, a self-service second-hand marketplace run by Chinese recycling company ATRenew.

Inside, rows of over 20,000 used phones are on display. Buyers scan QR codes for instant inspection reports and pricing, test the units and purchase in bulk.

The shop draws up to 1,000 visitors daily, with international traders making up about a third, said store manager Zhang Xiaoming.

Abdul Rahim, a 20-year-old shopkeeper who flies to China up to three times a month to stock his phone and accessory store in Algeria, capitalises on a price gap of 100 to 120 euros ($110 to $132) per device.

“It’s very easy for Algerians to get the visa to China. You put in your papers and in two or three days you have the visa in your passport,” he told AFP.

“For Europe, there just aren’t visas… So we come here.”

‘Buy, buy, buy’

Apple devices account for 70 to 80 per cent of sales, with the rest split among Chinese brands such as Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo, Zhang noted.

Older models like the iPhone 11, 12 and 13 — losing ground to cheap Androids in China — retain strong brand power overseas, where they find a second life, explained Jeremy Ji, ATRenew’s head of corporate strategy and overseas business.

At ATRenew’s massive processing hub in Dongguan, north of Shenzhen, roughly 30,000 second-hand gadgets arrive daily and are inspected and packed by over 300 technicians.

Rising prices are also changing buying habits in China itself, with consumers opting increasingly for pre-owned models, particularly nearly new premium models, said Arthur Guo, an analyst at IDC China.

Most phones discarded in China are still sold domestically, and bulk exports via official channels have not increased significantly, Lam, of Counterpoint, told AFP.

For Mama, sourcing phones is still a hands-on process.

“If I come, I spend a month checking (phones). I buy, buy, buy,” he said. “After I have finished, I go back to my country”.

item.title: Climate risk is financial risk. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement on December 12, 2015, climate change and its impact on the economy, industrialization, commerce, and trade have gained importance in policy formulation and the sustainable development agenda.
An important aspect of the agreement, particularly relevant to the financial sector, is Article 2.1(c), which calls for making financial flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development. This provision gives climate considerations a wider significance beyond environmental protection and places the alignment of financial resources with climate objectives within the broader framework of sustainable development.
Although the Paris Agreement does not prescribe guidance for individual lending decisions for commercial banks, its objectives provide an important policy direction for governments, regulators, and financial institutions.
As a signatory to the agreement, Bangladesh has also shifted its policy toward a low-carbon economy, and its banking sector has received new guidelines on sustainable finance -- including climate finance -- to build a climate-resilient economy.
The sustainable finance department (SFD) of Bangladesh Bank has progressively strengthened its policy framework for sustainable finance and climate-risk management. The department has also offered refinance schemes at lower interest rates to encourage banks and financial institutions to ensure the flow of funds into climate-friendly, low-carbon-emitting industrial establishments .
The economic cost of climate vulnerability
The German based Global Climate Risk Index ranked Bangladesh as the 13th most climate vulnerable country in 2026. The World Bank’s Country Climate and Development Report for Bangladesh (2022) identifies tropical cyclones, flooding, rising sea levels, extreme heat, and other climate-related hazards as significant threats to the country's development effort.
The report estimates that average tropical cyclones alone cost Bangladesh approximately$1 billion annually. It also warns that climate variability and extreme events could cause the loss of one-third of agricultural GDP by 2050. Under severe flooding scenarios, economic output could fall substantially below projected levels. The report further estimates that 13.3 million people could become internal climate migrants over the coming decades if climate impacts on agriculture, water availability, and coastal areas intensify.
In the World Bank report, An Unsustainable Life: The Impact of Heat on Health and the Economy of Bangladesh, it was said that Bangladesh's maximum temperature had increased by approximately 1.1°C since 1980, while the perceived temperature had risen by around 4.5°C. Heat-related health conditions and productivity losses resulted in an estimated 250 million lost workdays in 2024, with an economic cost of up to$1.78 billion, equivalent to approximately 0.4% of GDP.
These figures are very concerning for the banking sector. When economic activity is disrupted, borrowers' repayment capacity can deteriorate. A factory facing repeated production interruptions may experience declining revenue and rising operating costs. The consequences can appear in a bank's financial statements as increased overdue loans, higher credit impairment, reduced collateral values, and greater provisioning requirements.
Climate change affects financial performance of businesses, changes asset value, and disrupts supply chains, ultimately affecting the repayment capacity of the borrower. A flood can damage a factory, communication system, cause labour displacement which ultimately interrupts production, affect revenue and earnings. Salinity can affect agricultural output and the availability of freshwater. A cyclone can destroy infrastructure, disrupt transportation, supply chain, and deteriorate the cash flow of businesses.
These are not merely environmental consequences that can be considered temporary. They can directly affect a bank’s credit portfolio, earnings, and provision requirements.
These risks affect banks’ operations and credit portfolio in multiple ways depending on the borrower’s location, industry concentration of credit portfolio, business model, and capacity to adapt.
For example, a readymade garment manufacturing company located in an area exposed to recurrent flooding may have a sound financial position, however, repeated floods may damage machinery, interrupt production, increase insurance costs, and delay the delivery of export orders. This event may eventually affect its ability to service debt.
Enactment of new laws relating to carbon emission, environment protection, technological developments, market preferences, and investor expectations are principal sources of transition risk which can also affect the competitiveness and profitability of businesses.
More importantly, transition risks must be addressed from a global perspective. The ready-made garment sector is facing different carbon related regulations imposed by the buyers which forces them to consider upgrading environmental performance, energy efficiency, resource consumption, and sustainability standards. A factory that fails to invest in cleaner production, energy efficiency or improved environmental performance may face higher operating costs or lose business opportunities.
The transition to a low-carbon economy creates challenges, but it also generates investment opportunities. Renewable energy, energy-efficient industrial equipment, green buildings, cleaner production technologies, business automation, and sustainable transportation are areas where banks can play a significant financing role.
The gap between policy and credit decisions
Despite the introduction of regulatory guidelines and various sustainable finance initiatives by the central bank, an important implementation challenge remains: T ranslating climate-risk considerations into routine banking and credit decisions. B anks still treat climate change as an environmental and development issue, largely outside the conventional responsibilities of commercial banks.
In conventional credit appraisal, banks generally place considerable emphasis on the borrower's financial statements, projected income, cash-flow adequacy, debt-servicing capacity, profitability, leverage, collateral coverage, repayment history, and overall business prospects. Project financing decisions also rely on financial viability assessments and capital budgeting techniques.
These remain essential elements of sound lending. Social and environmental concerns including climate risk is addressed through regulatory clearances, environmental permits, and environmental and social due d iligence (ESDD).
Climate-risk assessment requires a broader perspective. It raises additional questions: Is the borrower's business located in an area exposed to recurrent flooding or extreme heat? Does the business depend heavily on water or other climate-sensitive resources? Could changes in environmental regulations or buyer requirements affect its competitiveness? Does the borrower have adequate measures to protect its assets and maintain business continuity? Most importantly, how could these vulnerabilities affect future cash flows, collateral values, and repayment capacity?
These are the questions that need to become part of the credit assessment process, particularly for sectors and geographical locations with significant climate exposure. To address all these issues, climate-risk considerations should become part of the bank's overall credit risk framework and must be considered as an integral part of risk governance.
The importance of climate stress testing
One of the most important tools to address climate risk is the climate stress testing. Banks can incorporate climate components and effects of their variability on income and asset value of the borrower in risk assessment metrics. Stress testing models can be designed to assess the impact of climate risk parameters on individual client level as well as to assess climate risk on the overall portfolio of the bank based on loan segregation on industries and concentration to different areas.
A useful approach to conduct climate stress testing should be to identify material climate-sensitive sectors, map portfolio exposure by geographical location and sector, assess the vulnerability of borrowers, and examine how different climate scenarios could affect their financial performance. The resulting analysis may help banks identify concentrations of risk that are not readily visible through conventional portfolio reporting.
However, climate stress testing to address climate risk at portfolio level as well as at individual borrower level in Bangladesh is not that easy to conduct overnight. It has practical challenges.
Reliable borrower-level location data, detailed climate projections, sector-specific vulnerability information, flood and rainfall related historical data, and suitable analytical models are not yet available across the market. Bangladesh Bank can take an initiative to develop a model for climate related stress testing.
Banks should therefore adopt a phased approach. Initial assessments can use available geographical and sectoral information, followed by progressively more sophisticated models as data quality and institutional capacity improve. At the initial stage, banks can introduce climate-risk screening into the credit appraisal process.
Adaptation finance: The overlooked aspect of climate finance
It is now evident that in most cases, banks use their resources in climate finance to mainly focus on climate risk mitigation -- particularly renewable energy, energy efficiency, installation of effluent treatment plants (ETP) aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emission. These investments remain important.
Mitigation finance supports activities that reduce or avoid greenhouse gas emissions while adaptation finance is very crucial to manage livelihoods of the most vulnerable communities.
However, for a climate-vulnerable country like Bangladesh, adaptation finance deserves equal attention. Adaptation finance supports investments that help businesses and communities prepare for and recover from climate-related impacts.
Examples include flood-resilient industrial infrastructure, improved drainage systems, rainwater harvesting, water-efficient irrigation, climate-resilient agricultural practices, improved storage facilities, saline-tolerant crop varieties, and climate-resilient infrastructure.
These investments may not always generate immediate financial returns in the conventional sense but their value often lies in preventing future losses, protecting productive assets, and maintaining business continuity.
The reason that the banks are not engaging more actively in scaling up adaptation finance is that the communities affected by climate change generally live far away from the banks. Moreover, economic vulnerability and financial fragility of the affected community, difficulties to identify bankable adaptation projects, uncertainty of financial return and repayment capacity, and a lack of technical knowledge to assess climate risk are also obstacles for banks to engage in adaptation finance.
What the banks can do
Considering the socio-economic importance of adaptation finance, banks must come forward with some practical market-oriented approach to address the issue.
Banks may be encouraged to set up specialized branches in climate-vulnerable areas where the staff shall be dedicated for selecting viable projects addressing the local adaptation needs.
For example, an agricultural enterprise could consider investments in water-efficient irrigation, improved drainage, climate-resilient storage, and other adaptation measures.
Similarly, financing a manufacturing company in a flood-prone area could include investment in flood protection, improved electrical infrastructure, elevated machinery, and business continuity arrangements.
Banking networks like sub-branch or agent banking outlets can be used to expand banking activities in remote climate sensitive areas. This will also reduce cost and help ensure financial inclusion and affinity with the local communities.
Banks should also invest in staff development. Relationship managers need to understand basic climate exposure and adaptation opportunities. Credit analysts need to know how climate-related factors may affect cash flow, collateral, and repayment capacity. Risk management teams need the capability to analyze portfolio concentration and conduct scenario-based assessments.
NGO-linked adaptation finance
One particularly promising approach for Bangladesh may be to establish an NGO- l inked climate adaptation finance m odel. This approach can address several barriers simultaneously, particularly discovering bankable projects, lack of collateral, high transaction costs, and limited access to vulnerable communities.
Under this arrangement, a commercial bank can provide wholesale financing to qualified NGOs, which subsequently extend adaptation financing to their existing beneficiaries. Banks need to develop special schemes and reporting guidelines for NGOs.
Policy support from central bank
It is not possible for commercial banks alone to address all the barriers independently. A supportive regulatory and institutional environment is necessary to encourage adaptation lending. The c entral bank must come forward with some initiatives. Moreover, rules regarding loan loss and provision requirements ought to be relaxed for climate finance exposure.
Understanding the nature of the investment
There is a fundamental distinction between commercially - viable adaptation investments and adaptation activities that primarily generate public benefits.
Consider the construction of climate - resilient infrastructure like a coastal ban k. This cannot be a commercial project. Banks should not be expected to finance every adaptation requirement through conventional loans schemes.
Projects that produce substantial social and economic benefits but require long payback and grace period s may require grants, government funding, or concessional blended finance. Mandatory climate risk f unds preserved by the commercial banks can be a good source of financing for projects of public interest.
Climate finance should not be viewed merely as an additional compliance obligation or a form of concessional lending. It should be recognized as a strategic credit risk management instrument. By financing adaptation measures today, banks can reduce the probability of future borrower distress, protect the quality of their loan portfolios, and contribute to the long-term resilience of the economy.
C limate finance therefore should not be treated simply as a reporting category or a numerical target. Banks need to develop commercially viable products that respond to the actual investment requirements of businesses.
